newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian church group blasts Arakis oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Canadian church group blasts Arakis oil deal.

text.p: A Canadian church group on Tuesday sharply criticised Calgary-based oil company Arakis Energy Corp. for signing a $1 billion oil deal with Sudan's Islamist government.

The Toronto-based Inter-Church Coalition on Africa, a group of seven mainstream churches, blasted Arakis for moving forward with the project despite what it called the Sudan government's "brutal" record on human rights.

"Arakis' work in Sudan lends legitimacy to a regime that has been condemned by the U.N. for genocide, slavery, indiscriminate bombing of civilians, killing of political opponents and forcing an extreme form of Islam on all Sudanese," the coalition said in a statement.

In a move anxiously awaited by its investors, Arakis and its partners on Saturday signed final agreements for the project, which includes development of a 12.2 million acre oil concession in southern Sudan and construction of a 900-mile (1,448-km) pipeline to the Red Sea from the oil fields.

Partners in the project, which is expected to start shipping as much as 250,000 barrels of oil a day by mid-1999, include Arakis with 25 percent, China National Petroleum Corp. with 40 percent, Malaysia state oil company Petronas with 30 percent and the Khartoum government with five percent.

For the past 13 years, Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war and hostilities were heightened early this year when rebel groups along the African nation's eastern borders launched an offensive against government troops.

"The revenues generated from oil sales will only help the Sudanese regime buy more weapons and fuel to fight the war and achieve its goal of stripping all Sudanese of their religious and cultural identities," coalition coordinator Gary Kenny said.

Arakis has often been threatened by Sudanese opposition forces, and last week the rebel Sudan Alliance Forces (SAF) described it and International Petroleum Corp., another Canadian firm operating in the country, as "vultures."
The SAF said it considered the foreign oil companies to be legitimate military targets.

However, Arakis Chief Executive John McLeod said on Tuesday that rebel threats had been a fact of life for his firm over the past two years but operations had never been attacked and security remained tight.
McLeod also said he believed Arakis could continue operating even if the Khartoum government was overthrown in what rebel forces hope will be a popular uprising.
"The likelihood of a rebel overthrow here, we feel, is very, very remote," he told a conference call.

"If they did, we are in Sudan as investors with our partners... What do you think the odds are of them kicking out that kind of a consortium if they want to go forward and have any kind of relations with the rest of the world?"

Kenny said the Canadian government has been a vocal critic of Sudan's record on human rights, but other than warning Arakis of the dangers of working in the country there was nothing it could do to bar the company from working there.

The coalition includes members from such religious groups as the Anglican Church of Canada, Canadian Catholic Organisation for Development and Peace, Evangelical Lutheran Church in Canada, Presbyterian Church in Canada and United Church of Canada.
